source.title: Dimensionality-Driven Learning with Noisy Labels
source.authors: Xingjun Ma; Yisen Wang; Michael E. Houle; Shuo Zhou; S. Erfani; Shu-Tao Xia; Sudanthi N. R. Wijewickrema; James Bailey

record.tranche_reason: The study varies symmetric label-noise rates and measures test accuracy, but does not report the random-label fitting or training-time outcomes in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on noisy labels and test accuracy. It does not report complete random-label training error, time to fit, unstructured inputs, regularization effects on random-label fitting, or a direct measure of learning shared patterns before memorizing noise. The cited findings from Zhang et al. (2017), Krueger et al. (2017), and Arpit et al. (2017) are prior work, not this study's results.
record.test_reason: Standard cross-entropy baselines test V4's test-performance trend under increasing label noise. Sections 3.3–3.4 also investigate V6 through training trajectories and a dimensionality-based account of early signal learning followed by noisy-label overfitting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors observe early dimensional compression followed by expansion associated with noisy-label overfitting, and propose LID-guided loss correction that suppresses expansion and achieves strong noisy-label classification performance. The explanation of early signal learning and later noisy-label accommodation is supported indirectly rather than by separate clean/noisy-example fitting curves.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies symmetric label-noise proportions and measures test accuracy; it does not reproduce the original random-label memorization experiments. Its method uses LID-based loss correction.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured test accuracy differs across dataset and symmetric label-noise rate.

fits_no_version.finding: D2L's comparative accuracy, lower representation dimensionality, lower critical sample ratio, and representation visualizations evaluate the proposed mitigation strategy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LID-guided loss correction improves robustness and representation quality under label noise.

record.problems: Table 1 reports test accuracy and standard deviation, but not training accuracy or training error. The study uses symmetric random label replacement at 0%, 20%, 40%, and 60%, not completely random labeling of the full training set.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 also reports Forward, Backward, Boot-hard, Boot-soft, and D2L test accuracy for each dataset and noise rate. These are comparisons of noisy-label learning strategies, rather than additional measurements of standard cross-entropy networks, so they are not included as rows for this claim.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error under that labeling, chance test performance, and unchanged training settings.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit across noise fractions and degradation through fully random labeling to chance. Table 1 stops at 60% incorrect labels; Figure 1's training-accuracy values are unavailable in the supplied text.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting and whether removing it harms clean-label generalization.
Direct, separate learning curves for correctly and incorrectly labeled examples; completely random-label training. The evidence here is an indirect dimensionality and generalization analysis.

missing.what: Early compression followed by expansion under 40% label noise, accompanied by initially rising and subsequently falling test accuracy; clean-label training instead shows decreasing dimensionality and stabilizing test accuracy. These are the study's own temporal results underlying its V6 interpretation.

Figure 1 includes training-accuracy trajectories for clean and 40%-corrupted MNIST and CIFAR-10 training. The record incorrectly implies training accuracy is never reported. Extract the curves before deciding whether they establish near-perfect training fit; numerical values cannot be recovered from the supplied text.

record.verdict_notes: Observed states for Table 1 refer to the measured test-degradation component, not verification of V4's entire conjunction. Increasing noise here means assigning selected examples one of the other class labels; the study does not reach completely random labeling. No original-source exclusion applies.

versions.untested_parts: Complete random labels, training error, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters are not tested.
Time to fit labels and convergence speed by corruption fraction are not reported.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs are not tested.

The study varies symmetric label-noise rates and reports test accuracy, but does not report whether training error stays perfect or near-perfect. Table 1 test-accuracy results are extracted; no training-fit result is reported.
The study does not test whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels, or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
The study discusses a two-stage dimensionality pattern and overfitting to noisy labels, but does not directly measure whether shared real-data patterns are learned before noisy labels are memorized.
